title: Tenant guidance — multiwave latency oscillation recap
content:
Overview:

This draft is a customer-facing recap and guidance note summarizing the multi-wave latency oscillation event that affected a subset of tenants across EU and US-West regions on 2029-02-19. The goal is to: (1) describe what happened in plain language, (2) provide an accurate timeline and impact summary, (3) explain root cause and mitigations we’ve applied, (4) list recommended customer actions to reduce exposure, and (5) outline next steps and compensation.

High-level summary (plain language):
- Between 2029-02-19 02:18 UTC and 2029-02-19 08:40 UTC, some customers saw repeated spikes in request latency and transient 5xx errors. The behavior was not a single outage but a sequence of latency waves tied to autoscaling and our in-memory prefix/KV cache eviction interactions, which created repeated queueing at the serving front-end.
- Impact: approximately 2.8% of production requests across affected regions experienced >2s latency spikes; ~0.6% returned 5xx. No customer data was deleted or corrupted.

Who was affected:
- Primary regions: eu-west-1 and us-west-2.
- Affected tenants: those pinned to variant-family v2.1 (models with large KV footprints) and those with high short-burst QPS patterns.
- Example symptoms seen by customers: intermittent slow responses, partial streaming stalls, and rare request failures with 500/503.

Customer-facing timeline (UTC):
- 02:10: Early signs — autoscaler observed rising tail latency on a small number of serving nodes; automatic scale-up initiated.
- 02:18: First visible latency wave — prefix cache eviction started on scaled nodes due to memory pressure. Rapid cache misses caused increased request compute and queueing.
- 03:05: Pattern repeats — as nodes re-entered steady-state, a coordinated eviction/rehydration pattern emerged (multi-wave oscillation).
- 04:30: Engineering mitigation #1 — we applied a conservative throttling policy at edge routers for very short-burst flows to reduce concurrent work and flatten the waves. Immediate reduction in peak latency observed.
- 05:10: Mitigation #2 — pinned a small subset of traffic to a lighter-weight model variant (v2.0-quant) for high-burst tenants; this reduced per-request memory pressure.
- 06:00: Work-in-progress patch deployed to autoscaler thresholds and the memory pressure detection heuristics to prevent reactive over-scaling that triggered eviction loops.
- 08:40: Stabilization — observed request latencies returned to normal baselines; monitoring shows no new waves.

Root cause (concise, customer-friendly):
- Interplay between autoscaler and our in-memory KV/prefix cache: When transient bursts triggered the autoscaler to add serving nodes, those nodes came online empty and quickly received traffic. That caused repeated large-volume cache fills and evictions across the fleet. A synchronization lag in KV replication and our eviction heuristics caused several coordinated eviction/reload cycles, producing repeated latency spikes.
- Contributing factors: (a) short-burst, high-concurrency customer workloads; (b) autoscaler thresholds tuned too aggressively for these patterns; (c) insufficient guardrails for prefix/KV cache warm-up under rapid fleet changes.

What we did (immediate mitigations):
- Edge throttling: short-burst request shaping to smooth concurrency and reduce simultaneous cold-cache work.
- Model variant pinning: offered automatic temporary routing to a compatible lower-memory variant for high-burst tenants.
- Autoscaler tuning: raised the scale-up threshold and increased stabilization window to avoid oscillatory scale events for short-lived spikes.
- Cache warm-up improvements: deployed incremental warm-up delays and staggered traffic ramp to new nodes to avoid synchronized cache filling.
- Observability: enabled additional high-cardinality metrics and request-level traces for affected tenants; we captured full logs and traces for audit and further analysis.

What we will do next (engineering roadmap items):
- Short term (1–2 weeks): refine memory-pressure heuristics, add a synthetic warm-up path for new nodes, and expand automatic fallback to lighter model variants for detected burst patterns.
- Medium term (4–8 weeks): implement leaderless KV sync improvements to reduce replication lag during rapid fleet changes and add a runtime-level admission controller to limit concurrent cold-cache builds.
- Long term (2–3 months): rework autoscaler to incorporate model-kv-footprint signals so scaling decisions account for expected cache warm-up cost.

Customer actions and recommended mitigations (what customers can do today):
- If you see similar short-burst high-QPS patterns: implement client-side short-term request pacing (small randomized jitter + exponential backoff) to avoid synchronized retries.
- Enable our per-tenant fallback option in the Console (Product → Hosted API → Routing) to allow automatic routing to a lower-memory-compatible variant during autoscale events. Contact support if you need help selecting a compatible variant.
- For customers using streaming: implement a small client-side window (e.g., 50–150ms) between parallel streams to avoid burst concurrency at the edge.
- Monitor: set an alert on p95 latency and 5xx rate and subscribe to region-specific health channels we’ll share below.

Data safety and logs:
- No customer payload storage was impacted. We did not see evidence of data loss or corruption.
- All traces and logs for affected windows have been archived and are available to customers on request for audit purposes. If you need a scoped packet of logs for your tenant, open a ticket with support and include your tenant-id and approximate timestamps.

Compensation and follow-up: 
- For customers materially impacted (defined as >1% error rate or >3x baseline p95 for a continuous 30m window during the event), we will apply a usage credit equivalent to 3 days of typical inference usage. Our CS team will follow up individually within 5 business days.

Communication plan and channels: 
- Public status page update: initial notice published 2029-02-19 02:45 UTC; follow-up update with mitigation summary at 07:00 UTC.
- Targeted tenant emails: CS to send personalized summaries to known materially impacted customers by 2029-02-20.
- Support escalation: customers affected can open an urgent ticket with support (support@redwood.ai) and include “IF-OSCILLATION-2029” in the subject for faster routing.

How we’ll prevent recurrence (customer-focused):
- We are adding conservative client-friendly controls (edge admission control and short-burst throttling) so tenant workloads like yours won’t trigger large-scale synchronous cache activity.
- We will add a Console toggle to enable ‘burst-moderation’ behavior per-tenant (ETA: 2–3 weeks) allowing you to opt into lower-latency guardrails for bursty patterns.

Questions we still have and open items for customers:
- We want to understand whether specific SDK versions or customer-side retry patterns correlated with increased exposure. If you can share your retry/backoff patterns or SDK version in a ticket, that helps our tuning.
- If you used any custom model pinning or non-default routing rules during the event, let us know so we can correlate behavior.

Contact and escalation: 
- Primary CS contact: Asha Patel (asha@redwood.ai) — customer post-incident owner.
- Engineering contact for technical deep dives: Marta Lopez (marta@redwood.ai).
- For urgent tickets: support@redwood.ai with subject prefix IF-OSCILLATION-2029.

Draft notes for status page snippets (short, copy-ready):
- 2029-02-19 02:45 UTC — Investigating: We’re investigating elevated latency and intermittent errors in EU and US-West regions affecting a subset of tenants. Engineers are on the case and mitigation is in progress.
- 2029-02-19 07:00 UTC — Mitigations applied: We’ve applied throttling and variant routing mitigations which have reduced peak latency. We’re monitoring for complete stabilization.
- 2029-02-19 08:45 UTC — Service stabilized: Latencies returned to baseline; ongoing follow-up and post-incident review in progress.

Attachment recommendations for customer packets:
- Tenant-specific trace bundle (on request).
- Short FAQ: what to do if you see intermittent 5xx, how to enable fallback variants, and contact points.

Approval/next steps (internal):
- CS to review wording and finalize personalized emails for materially impacted customers by 2029-02-20 EOD.
- Product to prioritize Console toggle for burst-moderation (scoped as P1 improvement).
- Eng to complete postmortem doc (CONFLUENCE-1234) and schedule technical review with SRE and Applied ML teams.

Notes to internal readers: keep customer language non-technical where possible; avoid internal-only terms except in the attached technical appendix. This draft will be converted into: (a) a short statuspage thread, (b) a templated tenant email, and (c) a technical appendix for customers who request deeper detail.

End of draft.
